Decoy slide the page has set aside

Decoy slide the page has set aside. The winter work of a second article stays in the tree and on the screen, with the eel traps lifted, the sluice boards stacked, and the wheel chocked so it cannot turn while the pond is empty. None of that is the page being read, however long it runs.

Decoy slide continued. The families who kept the decoy watch walked the banks at dusk and again before dawn, counting boards and listening for a leak, and the count was written on a slate that hung in the gear shed until the pond was filled again in the spring.

Decoy slide continued. A held article can outrun the one on screen by a wide margin and still be the wrong one to read: every extra sentence here exists so a score of raw text would pick this slide, and the read has to refuse it because the page marked the slide inert.

Decoy slide continued. The archive of that winter lists the nights the gate froze, the mornings the rope was stiff, and the afternoons the ice on the pond was thick enough to walk, none of which belongs in the reading of the article beside it.

Decoy slide continued. When the thaw came the boards went back in the order they had come out, the chocks came off the wheel, and the first turn of the season was slow because the bearings had sat dry since the last ebb of autumn.

Decoy slide continued. The slate in the gear shed was wiped for the new season only after the pond had held a full tide, which is the last line of a slide the page is still holding back.

Decoy slide continued. The ledger beside the slate names every tide the wheel turned that winter and every tide it did not, and the names are the reason this slide is longer than the article on screen: a count of characters would stop here, and the read has to keep going to the article the page actually has open.

Decoy slide continued. Boards, ropes, bearings, chocks, and the key to the gear shed are all listed twice, once for the putting away and once for the taking out, and the second list is written smaller because it was copied from the first on a cold morning.

Decoy slide continued. None of those lines is the mill pond the reader asked for. They stay in the document, they stay painted, and they stay unread for as long as the slide carries inert.

Fixed bar still on screen.

The overflow of this sentence is clamped and still read in full, including the words past the second line.

A tide mill fills a pond on the way in and empties it through a wheel on the way out. The families living nearest the water learned the sound of the gate the way other people learn a clock, and the shift changed when the tide did rather than when a bell did.

Millers slept in turns because the tide does not keep office hours. The gate opens on the flood, the pond takes what the sea will give, and the wheel is left to run until the level falls below the buckets and the stone slows to a stop.

Nothing about the work was written down at first. The order of the gates, the depth that meant a full pond, and the sound of a wheel running dry were carried by the people who slept beside it.

This paragraph sits below the fold and is still part of the page.

Pile one. The working notes of the mill fill a real box on the page and are long enough to be the body when no article is left to choose from, with the wheel and the pond and the gate all named in the notes the keeper kept by the door.

Pile two. Those notes list the mornings the rope was stiff and the evenings the pond was already full before the shift began, and they stay the notes even when a neighbouring box holds more words that the page has marked off.

Pile three. A box that is mostly a held slide must not win on the strength of the slide, so the notes here have to be chosen for the words that are actually in reach.

Pad one.

Pad two.

Pad three.

Padded slide one that must not decide which box is the page. The slide goes on about boards and ropes and a slate in a shed, and every extra line is weight a raw count would treat as the article. It is held back, and the box around it is not the page.

Padded slide two. More of the same held text, enough that this box outruns the notes beside it if the held part is allowed to count, which is the mistake the score has to refuse.

Padded slide three. The last of the held weight, still longer than the notes, still not the thing the page is offering to be read. The slide keeps going so the box that holds it is heavier, on a raw count, than the notes beside it, which is the whole of the trap.

Padded slide four. Another held paragraph of ropes, boards, and a slate, added so there is no tie to hide in and no way for the notes to win by being merely as long.
